patient.name: Patricia Doherty
patient.complaint: Two days of worsening breathlessness, now drowsy and confused

diagnosis.exam: Expect an arterial gas in the stem and 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause': PaO2 <8 kPa makes it respiratory failure, the PaCO2 (above or below 6 kPa) decides type 1 or type 2.

points: Patricia, 71, **COPD**: 3 days of green sputum and more wheeze.
Paramedics gave **15 L/min oxygen** via non-rebreather mask.
On the way in she became **drowsy and muddled**.
Daughter says she is 'never usually like this'.

steps.lead: Patricia's lungs are failing at both jobs: getting **oxygen in** and getting **CO2 out**.

points: Pursed-lip breathing, using her neck muscles.
A **coarse flap** when she holds her arms out.
Wheeze throughout, coarse crackles at the right base.

steps.q: Patricia has a coarse flap of her outstretched hands. What does it point to here?
steps.r: **Asterixis** in a COPD patient on high-flow oxygen means **CO2 retention**. Hypoxaemia alone causes cyanosis and confusion, not a flap.

steps.lead: Patricia shows the classic set: breathless, confused, drowsy and tachypnoeic, plus the **flap** that signals rising CO2.
Patricia's **COPD** is the commonest cause of **type 2** failure; a pneumonia patient with healthy lungs would more likely be type 1.

steps.title: Naming the failure from the gas
steps.caption: Two numbers, two questions. The PaCO2 decides the type.

steps.text: A saturation of **99% on 15 L** does not mean safe. Oxygen hides a rising CO2: **drowsiness plus a flap** means check an arterial gas now.
Drowsy plus flap in COPD is not 'just confusion from infection'. Think **CO2 narcosis** first, especially after uncontrolled oxygen.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (arterial blood gas) or 'initial investigation to find the cause' (chest X-ray; CTPA only when PE is suspected).

steps.q: Patricia is drowsy with a flap. Which test confirms respiratory failure and its type?
steps.r: Only an **ABG** gives PaO2, PaCO2 and pH. Oximetry misses CO2 completely.

steps.title: Arterial blood gas on 15 L/min oxygen
steps.text: High PaCO2 with acidosis: **acute-on-chronic type 2**. The raised bicarbonate shows she retains CO2 chronically.

steps.lead: Patricia's gas is the proof: **PaCO2 9.4 kPa** and **pH 7.24**. Her PaO2 looks fine only because she is on 15 L.

visual.title: PaCO2
visual.label: Patricia 9.4
visual.caption: Well above 6 kPa: hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure.

steps.lead: Now find why: Patricia needs a **chest X-ray**, bloods (FBC, CRP, U&E) and an ECG.

visual.title: Patricia's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation on hyperinflated lungs: an infective exacerbation of COPD.

points: ECG: sinus tachycardia 108 bpm, no acute changes.
No pleuritic pain or calf swelling: **no CTPA** needed.

steps.text: A normal SpO2 never excludes type 2 failure, and a venous gas cannot give you the PaO2. The **arterial** gas is the gold standard.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': controlled oxygen to the right target, then 'next step' NIV when pH is 7.25–7.35 in type 2, and intubation if NIV fails.

steps.q: Patricia's PaCO2 is 9.4 kPa on 15 L. What do you do with her oxygen now?
o: Switch to a 28% Venturi mask, target 88–92%
steps.r: She is a **CO2 retainer**: give controlled oxygen to **88–92%**. Never stop oxygen in a hypoxic patient.

steps.lead: Breathless, confused, abnormal gas: Patricia gets **oxygen immediately**, but controlled, not 15 L.

visual.title: Oxygen saturation target for Patricia
bands: too high for a CO2 retainer
visual.label: On 15 L: 99%
visual.caption: 99% is too high for Patricia. Titrate down into the 88–92% band.

steps.lead: Patricia's target is **88–92%**, and her cause is treated: antibiotics for the consolidation (plus nebulisers and steroids for the COPD exacerbation).

points: Nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium; oral prednisolone 30 mg.
Antibiotics started for the right lower zone consolidation.
Repeat ABG after 1 hour: **pH 7.29**, PaCO2 8.6 kPa.

visual.title: pH after 1 hour of treatment
bands: below 7.25: severe, low threshold to intubate
visual.label: Patricia 7.29
visual.caption: Still acidotic despite full medical treatment: start NIV.

steps.lead: Patricia's **pH 7.29** with type 2 failure after an hour of treatment is the textbook trigger for **NIV**.

steps.title: Escalation in type 2 respiratory failure
nodes: Worsening or no better: intubation and ventilation
steps.caption: Decide the ceiling of care early, before NIV starts.

steps.lead: Had Patricia's pH fallen on NIV or her GCS dropped, the next step would be **intubation and mechanical ventilation**. Repeat gases track her.

visual.title: Patricia's gases on NIV
visual.caption: pH rises as PaCO2 falls: NIV is working, no intubation needed.

steps.lead: Patricia's care follows the two rules examiners test: **88–92%** target for CO2 retainers and **NIV for pH 7.25–7.35**.

steps.text: NIV treats **type 2** acidotic failure. It is not the answer for type 1 failure from pneumonia, and a normal pH with a high CO2 (compensated) does not need it.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why PaCO2 stays normal in type 1, why COPD patients get lower oxygen targets, and how NIV clears CO2.

steps.lead: Patricia's consolidated right base is perfused but not ventilated: **V/Q mismatch** lowers her oxygen.

steps.title: Why type 1 keeps a normal CO2
nodes: Fluid or pus fills some alveoli
CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster than O2
Healthy alveoli clear CO2: PaCO2 normal or low

steps.lead: Patricia's real problem is ventilation: her COPD airways and tiring muscles cannot move enough air to **clear CO2**.

steps.q: Why did Patricia's CO2 rise on 15 L of oxygen?
steps.r: In a chronic CO2 retainer, uncontrolled oxygen **suppresses ventilation** (loss of hypoxic drive), so CO2 climbs.

steps.lead: Patricia relies partly on **hypoxic drive**, so the paramedics' 15 L pushed her CO2 up. Hence **88–92%**.
BiPAP pushed more air into Patricia with each breath and splinted her alveoli open, so her **PaCO2 fell**.
Patricia's flap and drowsiness are a **CO2 encephalopathy**; both settled as her PaCO2 came down.

steps.text: The exam loves the mechanism of a normal PaCO2 in type 1: **CO2 diffuses more readily than O2**, so healthy alveoli compensate.

mcq.q: Which arterial gas defines type 1 respiratory failure?
o: PaO2 <8 kPa, PaCO2 normal or low

mcq.q: What is the most important cause of type 2 respiratory failure?
mcq.r: **COPD** is the classic cause; the others usually cause type 1.

mcq.q: Which sign specifically suggests CO2 retention?
mcq.r: A coarse **flapping tremor** reflects CO2 encephalopathy.

mcq.q: Which is a cause of type 2 rather than type 1 respiratory failure?
mcq.r: **Opioids** depress respiratory drive, causing hypoventilation and a high CO2.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for respiratory failure?
mcq.r: The **ABG** gives PaO2, PaCO2 and pH.

mcq.q: Which first-line test identifies the underlying cause?
mcq.r: A **chest X-ray** (with bloods and ECG) looks for pneumonia, oedema or pneumothorax.

mcq.q: What saturation target is used in a patient at risk of CO2 retention?
mcq.r: **88–92%** for COPD or CO2 retainers; 94–98% for everyone else.

mcq.q: At what pH is NIV indicated in type 2 respiratory failure?
mcq.r: **NIV for pH 7.25–7.35** with a high CO2 despite initial treatment.

mcq.q: What is the next step when type 2 failure worsens on NIV?
mcq.r: Failure of NIV means **intubation and ventilation** (if within the ceiling of care).

mcq.q: Why is PaCO2 usually normal in type 1 respiratory failure?
o: CO2 diffuses more readily than O2
mcq.r: **CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster**, so working alveoli still clear it.

prompts.q: Define type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure with the gas cut-offs.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: PaO2 first, then PaCO2 decides the type.

points.p: Type 1: PaO2 <8 kPa with normal or low PaCO2
Type 2: PaO2 <8 kPa with PaCO2 >6 kPa
Failure to maintain oxygenation and/or ventilation

prompts.q: List the causes of type 1 respiratory failure.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these are lung problems with intact ventilation.

points.why: Ventilated but unperfused lung; CO2 is often low from hyperventilation.

prompts.q: List the causes of type 2 respiratory failure.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anything that stops air moving in and out.

points.why: Increased airway resistance and dead space.

points.p: Neuromuscular disease, e.g. motor neurone disease

prompts.q: What are the clinical features of respiratory failure, and which sign suggests CO2 retention?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a drowsy COPD patient with a flap is CO2 retention.

prompts.q: What is the gold-standard investigation and what does it show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: only the arterial gas gives you the PaCO2 and PaO2 together.

points.why: The PaCO2 tells you the type.

points.p: Acidosis depending on type and severity
points.why: A raised bicarbonate means chronic retention.

prompts.q: Which tests look for the underlying cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: confirm with ABG, then find the cause.

points.why: Only when the stem suggests PE.

prompts.q: What oxygen targets do you use, and how do you treat the cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: who is at risk of CO2 retention decides the target.

points.p: 88–92% for COPD or CO2 retention risk
Diuretics for pulmonary oedema; anticoagulation for PE

prompts.q: When is NIV used, and what if it fails?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the pH decides NIV versus intubation.

points.p: NIV (BiPAP) for type 2 failure with pH 7.25–7.35
points.why: Classically an acute exacerbation of COPD.

points.p: Not responding to NIV: intubation and mechanical ventilation

prompts.q: Why does type 1 failure occur and why is CO2 normal?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: V/Q mismatch plus the diffusion advantage of CO2.

points.p: CO2 diffuses more readily than O2

prompts.q: Why does type 2 occur, why is oxygen limited in COPD, and how does NIV help?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: it is all about ventilation.

points.p: COPD retainers rely on hypoxic drive; high O2 suppresses ventilation
NIV: inspiratory pressure augments tidal volume, expiratory pressure keeps alveoli open

points.why: Affects the reticular activating system and motor pathways.

glossary.Respiratory failure: Failure of the lungs to keep blood oxygen up and/or carbon dioxide down, defined by PaO2 below 8 kPa.
glossary.Type 1: Respiratory failure with low oxygen but normal or low carbon dioxide: an oxygenation problem.
glossary.Type 2: Respiratory failure with low oxygen and carbon dioxide above 6 kPa: a ventilation problem.
glossary.Hypoxaemia: Abnormally low oxygen level in arterial blood.
glossary.Hypercapnia: Abnormally high carbon dioxide level in arterial blood.
glossary.PaO2: Partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood; below 8 kPa defines respiratory failure.
glossary.PaCO2: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood; normal about 4.7 to 6.0 kPa.
glossary.ABG: Arterial blood gas: a sample from an artery giving pH, PaO2, PaCO2 and bicarbonate.
glossary.kPa: Kilopascal, the unit used for blood gas pressures in the UK.
glossary.Asterixis: A coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands, seen with CO2 retention and liver failure.
glossary.Cyanosis: Blue discolouration of the lips or skin from low blood oxygen.
glossary.COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: smoking-related fixed airflow obstruction, the commonest cause of type 2 failure.
glossary.ARDS: Acute respiratory distress syndrome: widespread inflammatory lung injury causing severe type 1 failure.
glossary.PE: Pulmonary embolism: a clot blocking a pulmonary artery.
glossary.Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lung alveoli, usually from left heart failure.
glossary.Motor neurone disease: Progressive degeneration of motor neurones that can weaken breathing muscles and cause type 2 failure.
glossary.V/Q mismatch: Mismatch between air reaching alveoli (ventilation) and blood flowing past them (perfusion), lowering oxygen transfer.
glossary.Hypoventilation: Breathing too little air per minute to clear carbon dioxide.
glossary.Minute ventilation: Total volume of air breathed per minute: tidal volume times breathing rate.
glossary.Dead space: Airway or lung that is ventilated but takes no part in gas exchange.
glossary.Hypoxic drive: Breathing stimulated by low oxygen, relied on partly by chronic CO2 retainers.
glossary.CO2 retainer: A patient, usually with severe COPD, whose blood CO2 runs chronically high.
glossary.NIV: Non-invasive ventilation: breathing support through a tight face mask without a tube in the airway.
glossary.NIPPV: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, another name for NIV.
glossary.BiPAP: Bilevel positive airway pressure: NIV with a higher pressure on breathing in and a lower one on breathing out.
glossary.IPAP: Inspiratory positive airway pressure on BiPAP; it boosts each breath to blow off CO2.
glossary.EPAP: Expiratory positive airway pressure on BiPAP; it holds alveoli open.
glossary.Tidal volume: Volume of air moved in or out in one normal breath.
glossary.Venturi mask: Oxygen mask delivering a fixed percentage of oxygen, such as 24% or 28%, used for CO2 retainers.
glossary.Non-rebreather mask: Mask with a reservoir bag giving high-concentration oxygen at 15 L/min.
glossary.Intubation: Passing a tube into the trachea so a machine can ventilate the lungs.
glossary.CTPA: CT pulmonary angiogram: contrast CT of the lung arteries to diagnose pulmonary embolism.
glossary.Metabolic encephalopathy: Brain dysfunction from a chemical disturbance such as high CO2, causing confusion and a flap.
glossary.Reticular activating system: Brainstem network that keeps us awake; CO2 retention depresses it, causing drowsiness.
glossary.Ceiling of care: The agreed highest level of treatment for a patient, for example ward-based NIV but not intubation.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man with COPD has 3 days of increasing breathlessness and a cough productive of green sputum. He is drowsy and has a coarse flapping tremor. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 150/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis from a blood gas: is PaO2 below 8 kPa, and is PaCO2 above 6 kPa?
PaO2 6.8 (<8) = respiratory failure. PaCO2 8.2 (>6) = hypercapnia. COPD, drowsiness and a flap all fit CO2 retention.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low oxygen and high CO2 with acidosis in COPD: **type 2 respiratory failure**.

elim: The pH is low but the CO2 is high, so the acidosis is respiratory, not metabolic.
pH is acidotic; the raised bicarbonate is renal compensation for chronic CO2 retention.
Alkalosis needs pH above 7.45 and a low CO2.
Type 1 needs a normal or low PaCO2; this is 8.2 kPa.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 respiratory failure.** Rule: PaO2 <8 kPa + PaCO2 >6 kPa = type 2.

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman with COPD is brought in confused and drowsy after 2 days of increasing breathlessness. She has a flapping tremor. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 138/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L/min oxygen via nasal cannulae.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: which test proves respiratory failure and tells you the type?
A COPD patient who is drowsy with a flap is retaining CO2. A reassuring SpO2 says nothing about CO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Only the **arterial blood gas** measures PaCO2, PaO2 and pH.

elim: The X-ray finds the cause, but cannot confirm respiratory failure.
CTPA is only for suspected PE; nothing here suggests it.
Peak flow is for asthma monitoring and is unsafe to rely on in a drowsy patient.
Spirometry diagnoses COPD when stable, not acute failure.

steps.x: **A. Arterial blood gas.** Rule: drowsy COPD patient = ABG, whatever the saturation.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man with an acute exacerbation of COPD has received 28% oxygen via Venturi mask, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone and antibiotics. One hour later his respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89%.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: Next step after full medical treatment: look at the pH.
Type 2 failure with pH 7.30 despite optimal medical treatment for an hour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: pH 7.25–7.35 with high CO2: **NIV**.

elim: High-flow oxygen would worsen hypercapnia; target stays 88–92% and sats are 89%.
Aminophylline is not the next step for persistent acidosis.
Intubation is for NIV failure or pH that is falling below 7.25 with deterioration.
He has already had nebulisers; the acidosis needs ventilatory support.

steps.x: **D. Non-invasive ventilation.** Rule: type 2, pH 7.25–7.35 after initial treatment = NIV.

technique.stem: A 78 year old woman with severe COPD is given 15 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask by paramedics. Over 40 minutes she becomes increasingly drowsy. Her oxygen saturation is 99%. An arterial gas shows PaCO2 10.2 kPa (4.7–6.0) and pH 7.21 (7.35–7.45).
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her rising PaCO2?
o: Loss of hypoxic drive to breathe

steps.x: A mechanism question: why did CO2 rise after oxygen was given?
A chronic CO2 retainer given uncontrolled high-flow oxygen, then CO2 narcosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: She relies on **hypoxic drive**; high oxygen suppresses ventilation and CO2 climbs.

elim: Oxygen does not increase CO2 production.
The pH is 7.21: this is acidosis, not alkalosis.
Oxygen toxicity takes much longer and causes lung injury, not acute hypercapnia.
PE causes type 1 failure with a low CO2.

steps.x: **B. Loss of hypoxic drive.** Rule: COPD + high-flow oxygen + drowsy = CO2 retention; target 88–92%.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man has 4 days of fever, cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He has no past medical history. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: PaO2 7.1 kPa (<8) with a low PaCO2 is type 1 respiratory failure, here from pneumonia. The low CO2 and mild alkalosis come from tachypnoea, not anxiety.

steps.x: Name the gas abnormality: start with the PaO2.
PaO2 below 8 = respiratory failure. PaCO2 low, so not type 2. Pneumonia in healthy lungs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Type 1 respiratory failure** from pneumonia.

elim: Bicarbonate is normal; the alkalosis is respiratory from tachypnoea.
Hyperventilation syndrome has a normal PaO2; this patient is hypoxaemic.
PaO2 of 7.1 kPa is far from normal.
Type 2 needs PaCO2 above 6 kPa.

steps.x: **D. Type 1 respiratory failure.** Rule: low O2, low or normal CO2 = type 1.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man is found unresponsive in a hostel room. He has pinpoint pupils and needle track marks on both forearms. His pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 6 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 81% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his respiratory failure?
practice.e: Pinpoint pupils, track marks and a respiratory rate of 6 give type 2 failure from reduced respiratory drive: opioid toxicity. Normal bicarbonate shows it is acute.

steps.x: A cause question: decide the type first, then match it.
High CO2 with a very slow rate = hypoventilation from depressed drive. Pupils and track marks point to opioids.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute type 2 failure from **opioid toxicity**.

elim: Asthma gives a fast respiratory rate and wheeze, not a rate of 6 with miosis.
Guillain-Barré causes type 2 failure but over days with ascending weakness, not pinpoint pupils.
Pneumonia causes type 1 with fever and tachypnoea.
PE causes type 1 failure with a low CO2.

steps.x: **C. Opioid toxicity.** Rule: slow breathing + high CO2 + pinpoint pupils = opioids.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with COPD is admitted with an infective exacerbation. He is drowsy. His pulse rate is 106 bpm, BP 144/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% on 28% oxygen. His arterial PaCO2 is 9.6 kPa (4.7–6.0).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: CO2 retention causes asterixis (a coarse flap) and warm, vasodilated peripheries. Pinpoint pupils would suggest opioids, not CO2.

steps.x: An examination finding: which sign goes with a high CO2?
Hypercapnia in COPD: a CO2 encephalopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A coarse **flapping tremor** (asterixis).

elim: CO2 vasodilates: peripheries are warm with a bounding pulse.
Pinpoint pupils suggest opioid toxicity, not COPD.
Spider naevi point to chronic liver disease.
Tracheal deviation suggests tension pneumothorax or collapse.

steps.x: **A. Asterixis.** Rule: CO2 retention = flap, warm hands, bounding pulse, drowsiness.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with motor neurone disease has 2 months of morning headaches, daytime sleepiness and breathlessness when lying flat. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Weak respiratory muscles cause hypoventilation: PaO2 <8 kPa with PaCO2 >6 kPa is type 2 respiratory failure. Morning headaches are classic of nocturnal CO2 retention.

steps.x: A diagnosis from the gas, in a neuromuscular patient.
Low O2, high CO2. Neuromuscular weakness causes hypoventilation, worse at night.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Type 2 respiratory failure** from MND.

elim: Hyperventilation lowers CO2; this CO2 is high.
The acidosis is respiratory (high CO2) and the bicarbonate is raised, not low.
PE causes type 1 with a low CO2 and sudden onset.
Type 1 needs a normal or low PaCO2.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 respiratory failure.** Rule: neuromuscular disease is a classic type 2 cause.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman with ischaemic heart disease wakes at night acutely breathless. She has bibasal crackles and a raised JVP. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 168/96 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her respiratory failure?
practice.e: Type 1 failure (low O2, low CO2) with crackles, raised JVP and bilateral perihilar shadowing is pulmonary oedema. COPD, opioids and MND cause type 2.

steps.x: A cause question: type first, then the clinical picture.
Low O2, low CO2 = type 1. Heart disease, crackles, JVP and the X-ray = fluid in the alveoli.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 1 failure from **pulmonary oedema**.

elim: COPD gives type 2 with a high CO2 and wheeze.
MND causes slow type 2 hypoventilation.
Opioids cause type 2 with a slow respiratory rate.
Pneumothorax gives unilateral absent breath sounds and a visible lung edge.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary oedema.** Rule: pneumonia, oedema, PE and ARDS are the type 1 causes.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man who has smoked 40 cigarettes a day for 45 years has 3 days of worsening breathlessness and wheeze. He has a barrel chest and uses pursed-lip breathing. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 140/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his respiratory failure?
practice.e: Type 2 failure with a raised bicarbonate in a heavy smoker with wheeze, barrel chest and pursed lips is an acute exacerbation of COPD, the most important type 2 cause.

steps.x: Underlying cause: decide the type, then match the history.

clues: smoked 40 cigarettes a day for 45 years
steps.x: High CO2 with chronic compensation (HCO3 31) in a heavy smoker with hyperinflation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 2 failure from an **acute exacerbation of COPD**.

elim: Hyperventilation gives a low CO2 and normal PaO2.
Interstitial lung disease causes type 1 failure with fine crackles.
PE causes type 1 failure with a low CO2.
Pulmonary oedema causes type 1 failure with crackles and raised JVP.

steps.x: **A. Acute exacerbation of COPD.** Rule: COPD is the most important cause of type 2.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman has 3 days of fever and productive cough. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. An arterial gas confirms type 1 respiratory failure.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: Once the ABG confirms respiratory failure, a chest X-ray is the first-line test for the cause; fever and productive cough suggest pneumonia. CTPA is only for suspected PE.

steps.x: The failure is confirmed; now the first test for the cause.
Infection is the likely cause; the gas is already done.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest X-ray** plus bloods.

elim: Bronchoscopy is invasive and not first-line.
CTPA is for suspected PE: no pleuritic pain, leg swelling or risk factors given.
Spirometry is for chronic airway disease, not acute illness.
V/Q scanning is a PE test, used when CTPA is unsuitable.

steps.x: **B. Chest X-ray.** Rule: ABG confirms the failure, CXR finds the cause.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has sudden breathlessness and right pleuritic chest pain 4 days after a long-haul flight. Her left calf is swollen. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Her chest X-ray is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause of her respiratory failure?
practice.e: Type 1 failure with a normal chest X-ray, pleuritic pain, recent flight and a swollen calf means suspected PE, so CT pulmonary angiogram is the test.

steps.x: Which test finds the cause, given a normal X-ray?
Type 1 failure, DVT and a clear X-ray: think PE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT pulmonary angiogram**.

elim: Bronchoscopy looks at airways, not pulmonary arteries.
Cardiac MRI is not used to diagnose acute PE.
HRCT is for interstitial lung disease, without contrast in the arteries.
Spirometry does not diagnose acute PE.

steps.x: **C. CTPA.** Rule: CT is the additional test when PE is suspected.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with known COPD and previous hypercapnic admissions has an infective exacerbation. He is alert. His pulse rate is 102 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 83% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?
o: High-flow oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask
practice.e: A known CO2 retainer needs controlled oxygen via Venturi mask to 88–92%. High-flow oxygen or a 94–98% target risks worsening hypercapnia; NIV needs a gas showing acidosis first.

steps.x: Initial oxygen: who is at risk of CO2 retention?
Hypoxic, so oxygen now; a CO2 retainer, so controlled oxygen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Uncontrolled high flow suppresses ventilation and raises CO2.
He is alert; intubation is for NIV failure.
94–98% is the target for patients without CO2 risk.
NIV comes after a gas shows pH 7.25–7.35 despite treatment.

steps.x: **E. Venturi mask targeting 88–92%.** Rule: COPD retainer = 88–92%.

practice.stem: A 24 year old woman with no past medical history has 2 days of fever and cough. Chest X-ray shows left lower zone consolidation. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate oxygen prescription?
o: Room air with repeat gas in 1 hour
practice.e: Type 1 failure in a young woman with no CO2 retention risk: oxygen to 94–98%, plus antibiotics for the pneumonia. 88–92% is only for patients at risk of hypercapnia.

steps.x: An oxygen target: is she at risk of CO2 retention?
Type 1 failure from pneumonia; no COPD, low CO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oxygen to **94–98%**.

elim: Intubation is for refractory failure; she has not had oxygen yet.
NIV is for type 2 acidotic failure.
88–92% is for CO2 retainers only.
Withholding oxygen in a hypoxic patient is unsafe.

steps.x: **D. Oxygen targeting 94–98%.** Rule: no CO2 risk = 94–98%.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with COPD has been on non-invasive ventilation for 2 hours for type 2 respiratory failure. She is now increasingly drowsy with a GCS of 8. For full escalation. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue NIV and repeat the arterial gas in 4 hours
practice.e: Worsening acidosis and falling GCS despite NIV means NIV has failed; she is for full escalation, so intubation and mechanical ventilation.

steps.x: Next step after NIV: is it working?
pH falling and CO2 rising on NIV, GCS 8: NIV failure, and no ceiling on care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Intubation and mechanical ventilation**.

elim: Waiting 4 hours on failing NIV risks arrest.
High-flow oxygen worsens hypercapnia and does not ventilate.
Aminophylline will not reverse established ventilatory failure.
Steroids treat the exacerbation but not the immediate failure.

steps.x: **D. Intubation and mechanical ventilation.** Rule: severe, not responding to NIV = intubate.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man with lobar pneumonia has an oxygen saturation of 86% breathing air. His respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute. An arterial gas shows PaO2 7.2 kPa (10–13) and PaCO2 4.3 kPa (4.7–6.0).
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his PaCO2 not being raised?
o: Carbon dioxide diffuses more readily than oxygen
practice.e: In type 1 failure, V/Q mismatch impairs oxygen transfer, but CO2 diffuses much more readily, so the remaining alveoli and tachypnoea keep PaCO2 normal or low.

steps.x: A mechanism: why is CO2 normal when O2 is low?
Type 1 failure from consolidation: V/Q mismatch.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CO2 diffuses more readily than O2**, so ventilated alveoli clear it.

elim: Hypoxic drive matters in COPD retainers and raises CO2 when lost.
More dead space raises CO2 rather than keeping it low.
Fever increases, not reduces, CO2 production.
The kidneys handle bicarbonate; CO2 is cleared by the lungs.

steps.x: **A. CO2 diffuses more readily.** Rule: type 1 = V/Q mismatch with CO2 cleared.
